articles.title_original: Physiological Trajectories and Observation Patterns in ICU Mortality Prediction: Transportability Under Changing Measurement Conditions
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.42126v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Objective: To examine how changes in clinical measurement practices affect the transportability of predictive information from physiological trajectories and observation patterns in longitudinal ICU records.
  Methods: In-hospital mortality was predicted using measurements from the first 48 hours of ICU admission in MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. Nested representations captured the latest physiological state (R1), trajectory summaries (R2), and observation timing and frequency (R3). Models trained on 7,762 MetaVision patients were evaluated on 21,682 MIMIC-IV and 43,878 eICU patients from 204 hospitals. Restriction experiments tested measurement timing at matched counts and reduced availability.
  Results: Physiological trajectories improved prediction beyond latest values across settings, including transfer to eICU (R2-R1 log-loss difference -0.01446, 95% CI -0.01701 to -0.01202). Observation patterns improved prediction following transfer to MIMIC-IV (R3-R2 -0.00564) and in locally developed eICU models (-0.00402, 95% CI -0.00517 to -0.00283), but not clearly following transfer from MetaVision to eICU (+0.00106, 95% CI -0.00087 to +0.00355). At matched observation counts, retaining measurements spread throughout the 48-hour window reduced log loss relative to random retention, more for R3 than R2 (0.04324 versus 0.00721). R3 was also more sensitive to the loss of recent measurements. Retraining under reduced availability restored its advantage over R2.
  Conclusions: Physiological trajectories transferred consistently, while observation patterns offered less reliable benefits and greater sensitivity to measurement timing and availability. Their transferability may depend on diversity of measurement practices during training. Clinical prediction models should be evaluated across measurement conditions as well as patient populations.

articles.title_original: Generative Forecasting from Coarse Observations: Does Cascading Help?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.00686v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants can make substantial distributional errors when trained over the full forecast horizon with finite data and model capacity, despite being exact in principle. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets stronger, and increases as the dependence of the forecast on the observation becomes more oscillatory. Consistent with our experiments, cascading is detrimental when the direct forecast is "easy" to learn, for example Gaussian as in the passive scalar case. We release our datasets as a first benchmark for probabilistic forecasting with ground-truth conditional ensembles.

articles.title_original: Best-of-Depth: Learning Exploratory Dynamics in Looped Transformers
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.04663v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent-state updates, but final-depth training does not directly encourage useful intermediate alternatives. We introduce Best-of-Depth (BoD), which trains a recurrent trajectory as a candidate set by minimizing prediction loss across depths. Different valid targets can be matched at different depths without architectural changes or depth-specific labels. An exact-match analysis connects this objective to solution coverage. On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training. Further experiments show discovery beyond the training depth and recovery of solutions withheld from teacher pools on familiar inputs. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated separately at evaluated fixed depths. These results support training recurrent computation for solution discovery along its trajectory.

articles.title_original: The Alignment Tax Is Graded: Task-Selective Capability Loss Under Length-Normalized DPO with SFT Retention
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.06476v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Setting. This is an empirical characterization study; we propose no new method and run no comparisons against alternative objectives. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B with sparse LoRA and length-normalized DPO plus an SFT retention term (the RPO objective) on structured financial-filing tasks, and track downstream capability as the implicit reward margin grows to $\sim 7$ $\beta$-scaled units (nf4 training; $\sim 3$ under fp16 measurement on the unquantized base). Question. Does margin growth degrade capability uniformly across tasks, or selectively? Findings. In a pre-registered study (8 seeds, 6 unseen at freeze) with artifact-aware scoring and TOST equivalence testing, the alignment tax is graded and task-selective: extraction is preserved ($\Delta = -0.55$ pts, equivalent at $\pm5$ pts), json loses little ($\Delta = -3.52$ pts, equivalence fails on a clustered item-level interval), and router degrades severely ($\Delta = -30$ pts). Router's loss concentrates in a margin 1-3 damage window containing a transient format-break spike. The margin is accounted for almost entirely ($\geq 96\%$) by suppression of rejected completions, with chosen reward approximately flat, consistent with the retention term anchoring it; we do not attribute the behavioral damage to any single gradient channel. Gold-logp deflation is task-selective (extraction $-0.15$, json $-1.04$, router $-1.47$ nats/token under fp16), with gold selectively protected relative to incorrect controls on extraction (8/8 seeds). QLoRA reward margins differ up to $3.4\times$ between nf4 training and unquantized fp16 measurement, with an axis-dependent gap. Scope. Length-normalized rewards with SFT retention, sparse LoRA on 8/32 layers, one 4B model, easily-separable synthetic preferences, three structured tasks. A no-retention control and a measured format-alignment metric are left to future work.

articles.title_original: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.06837v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.

articles.title_original: Attention at Absolute Zero
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.11937v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.

articles.title_original: When Does Causality Help in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.15073v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, yet the literature rarely states when it helps. Holding one causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) fixed, we vary graph quality, anomaly type and protocol against ground truth. Graph quality fixes the payoff: on a twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. Anomaly type fixes the target: the structural factor lifts window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, and its advantage vanishes below a break severity s 0.3. Protocol fixes the ranking: point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while range-aware VUS separates the autoencoder family from the classical baselines. On real benchmarks the causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and cross-subsample reproducibility selects entities inside it; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC. The structural factor also transfers to classical detectors .

articles.title_original: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.17108v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Memory determines which large language models (LLMs) an edge device can run and how fast it runs them: capacity limits a 4 GB Jetson Nano, and bandwidth limits an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed weight formats (GPTQ, AWQ, and the GGUF K- and I-quants) spend the same number of bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. We present LazyWeights, which keeps these formats, tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At 1% and 3.5% perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are 5.7-31.4% smaller than the best GGUF format. A bit-exact 0.21 mm^2 ASIC decoder unit (1 GHz, 7 nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to 36% and 38% (54% and 44% with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, LazyWeights needs 58-64% less time and 53-57% less energy per token than the GGUF runtime on the CPU, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6x faster at 3.89 bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput, and the unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

articles.title_original: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.17794v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

articles.title_original: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.18639v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

articles.title_original: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.19597v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints.
  We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure.
  NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

articles.title_original: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.22098v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

articles.title_original: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.23035v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

articles.title_original: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.24757v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree.
  In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

articles.title_original: Variance Reduction for Matrix Computations with Applications to Gaussian Processes
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2106.14565v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In addition to recent developments in computing speed and memory, methodological advances have contributed to significant gains in the performance of stochastic simulation. In this paper we focus on variance reduction for matrix computations via matrix factorization. We provide insights into existing variance reduction methods for estimating the entries of large matrices. Popular methods do not exploit the reduction in variance that is possible when the matrix is factorized. We show how computing the square root factorization of the matrix can achieve in some important cases arbitrarily better stochastic performance. In addition, we detail a factorized estimator for the trace of a product of matrices and numerically demonstrate that the estimator can be up to 1,000 times more efficient on certain problems of estimating the log-likelihood of a Gaussian process. Additionally, we provide a new estimator of the log-determinant of a symmetric positive-definite matrix where the log-determinant is treated as a normalizing constant of a probability density.

articles.title_original: Designing Algorithmic Recommendations to Achieve Human-AI Complementarity
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2405.01484v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Algorithms frequently assist, rather than replace, human decision-makers. However, the design and analysis of algorithms often focus on predicting outcomes and do not explicitly model their effect on human decisions. This discrepancy between the design and role of algorithmic assistants becomes particularly concerning in light of empirical evidence that suggests that algorithmic assistants again and again fail to improve human decisions. In this article, we formalize the design of recommendation algorithms that assist human decision-makers without making restrictive ex-ante assumptions about how recommendations affect decisions. We formulate an algorithmic-design problem that leverages the potential-outcomes framework from causal inference to model the effect of recommendations on a human decision-maker's binary treatment choice. Within this model, we make a connection between algorithmic recommendations and instrumental variables. Leveraging this connection, we introduce a monotonicity assumption that leads to an intuitive classification of human responses to the algorithm. Under this assumption, we can express the human's response to algorithmic recommendations in terms of their compliance with the algorithm and the active decision they would take if the algorithm sends no recommendation. We showcase the utility of our framework using an online experiment that simulates a hiring task. We argue that our approach can make sense of the relative performance of different recommendation algorithms in the experiment and can help design solutions that realize human-AI complementarity. Finally, we leverage our approach to derive maximin-optimal recommendation algorithms that can be implemented with machine learning using limited training data.

articles.title_original: CP-Guard+: A New Paradigm for Malicious Agent Detection and Defense in Collaborative Perception
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2502.07807v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Collaborative perception (CP) is a promising method for safe connected and autonomous driving, which enables multiple vehicles to share sensing information to enhance perception performance. However, compared with single-vehicle perception, the openness of a CP system makes it more vulnerable to malicious attacks that can inject malicious information to mislead the perception of an ego vehicle, resulting in severe risks for safe driving. To mitigate such vulnerability, we first propose a new paradigm for malicious agent detection that effectively identifies malicious agents at the feature level without requiring verification of final perception results, significantly reducing computational overhead. Building on this paradigm, we introduce CP-GuardBench, the first comprehensive dataset provided to train and evaluate various malicious agent detection methods for CP systems. Furthermore, we develop a robust defense method called CP-Guard+, which enhances the margin between the representations of benign and malicious features through a carefully designed Dual-Centered Contrastive Loss (DCCLoss). Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on both CP-GuardBench and V2X-Sim, and demonstrate the superiority of CP-Guard+.

articles.title_original: LLM-Based Threat Detection and Prevention Framework for IoT Ecosystems
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2505.00240v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced complex and evolving cybersecurity challenges. This paper presents a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for intelligent threat detection and prevention in IoT networks. The proposed architecture integrates two core components: a Detection Component that leverages fine-tuned models trained on IoT-specific datasets (IoT-23 and TON_IoT) to identify anomalous network behaviours, and a Prevention Component that generates adaptive response strategies to mitigate detected threats. The framework incorporates prompt management, local adaptation, and global refinement modules to support context-aware decision-making and continuous model-guided adaptation. Experimental validation in a Docker-based edge-cloud environment shows that BERT Small achieves 99.75% accuracy, F1-score, precision, and recall for threat detection, while the Prevention LLM achieves 98.3% accuracy in selecting suitable mitigation actions. These results highlight the potential of LLM-driven architectures to provide explainable and adaptive security solutions for next-generation IoT ecosystems.

articles.title_original: FlowDrive: moderated flow matching with data balancing for trajectory planning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2509.21961v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Learning-based planners are sensitive to the long-tailed distribution of driving data. Common maneuvers dominate datasets, while dangerous or rare scenarios are sparse. This imbalance can bias models toward the frequent cases and degrade performance on critical scenarios. To tackle this problem, we compare balancing strategies for sampling training data and find reweighting by trajectory pattern an effective approach. We then present FlowDrive, a flow-matching trajectory planner that learns a conditional rectified flow to map noise directly to trajectory distributions with few flow-matching steps. We further introduce moderated, in-the-loop guidance that injects small perturbation between flow steps to systematically increase trajectory diversity while remaining scene-consistent. On nuPlan and the interaction-focused interPlan benchmarks, FlowDrive achieves state-of-the-art results among learning-based planners and approaches methods with rule-based refinements. After adding moderated guidance and light post-processing (FlowDrive*), it achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across nearly all benchmark splits. Our code is available at https://github.com/einsteinguang/flow_drive_planner.

articles.title_original: Survival of the fittest Cox model: Pivotal variable selection for time-to-event data
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2510.19374v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We revisit Cox's proportional hazards model to improve variable selection in survival analysis. A square-root transformation of the partial likelihood renders the selection of the regularization parameter asymptotically pivotal: the baseline hazard and the censoring rate cancel exactly, and the way censoring is spread over time only enters through a bounded correction of order $1/\log n$. Using martingale residuals, we compute this penalty level by Monte Carlo without reordering the design matrix. The resulting criterion borrows from information criteria such as BIC and from penalized regression methods such as the lasso, taking the best of both. On simulated and real data, our method substantially improves upon state-of-the-art approaches used daily.

articles.title_original: Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2510.21798v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior.
  In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.

articles.title_original: Sparse corruption in low-rank matrix inference: the PCA benchmark
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2511.11927v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard tool for extracting a low-rank signal from noisy observations. It is known that when applying PCA to a rank-one signal corrupted by a dense, homogeneous noise, in the large matrix size limit, the BBP transition occurs, where the emergence of an outlying eigenvalue and the alignment of the corresponding eigenvector occur at the same critical signal strength. Here we study the case of sparse noise corruption. The noise matrix is modelled as the adjacency matrix of a weighted undirected graph with finite average connectivity. Using the replica method, we analytically compute the typical top eigenvalue, the top eigenvector component density, and the overlap with the signal, through recursive distributional equations solved by population dynamics. We identify two signal-strength transitions as functions of graph connectivity: $\theta_{\rm crit}$, marking signal recovery by the top eigenvector and generalising the BBP transition, and $\theta_{\rm b}$, where the signal-related eigenvalue detaches from the bulk. For noise with nonzero mean, these transitions need not coincide because of a structural sparse-graph outlier, leading to a discontinuous transition in the overlap with the top eigenvector. For a Random Regular degree distribution, we obtain exact closed-form expressions for both thresholds, the signal eigenvalue and the squared overlap, and show that the same formulas also predict the overlap of the signal with the second eigenvector in the intermediate regime $\theta_{\rm b}<\theta\leq \theta_{\rm crit}$. For a Poissonian degree distribution, an approximate closure of the recursions yields fast and accurate predictions in the recovery phase that agree with exact results from population dynamics. We also recover dense-noise results in the large-connectivity limit, and validate the theory by numerical diagonalisation of large matrices.

articles.title_original: Variational analysis of determinantal varieties
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2511.22613v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Determinantal varieties---the sets of bounded-rank matrices or tensors---have attracted growing interest in low-rank optimization. The tangent cone to low-rank sets is widely studied and underpins a range of geometric methods. The second-order geometry, which encodes curvature information, is more intricate. In this work, we develop a unified framework to derive explicit formulas for both first- and second-order tangent sets to various low-rank sets, including low-rank matrices, tensors, symmetric matrices, and positive semidefinite matrices. The framework also accommodates the intersection of a low-rank set and another set satisfying some assumptions, thereby yielding a tangent intersection rule. Through the lens of tangent sets, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition under which a nonsmooth problem and its smooth parameterization share equivalent second-order stationary points. As applications, we exploit tangent sets to characterize optimality conditions for low-rank optimization and prove that verifying second-order optimality is NP-hard. Moreover, for low-rank semidefinite programs, the Burer--Monteiro parameterization maps fourth-order stationary points of the parameterized problem to second-order stationary points of the original problem. In a separate line of analysis, we investigate variational geometry of the graph of the normal cone to matrix varieties, deriving the explicit Bouligand tangent cone, Fr\'echet and Mordukhovich normal cones to the graph. These results are further applied to develop optimality conditions for low-rank bilevel programs.

articles.title_original: Quantum Nondecimated Wavelet Transform: Theory, Circuits, and Applications
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.21478v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The quantum nondecimated wavelet transform uses a shift register to apply circular shifts to an amplitude encoded signal before a single orthogonal wavelet transform. We show that tracing out the shift register gives level probabilities equal to the normalized nondecimated wavelet energies, invariant under circular shifts. Its diagonal gives moving averages of squared coefficients. We derive a multinomial model for the level counts and show how to read the autocovariance at lag one for all but the coarsest detail level. For these global statistics, direct Fourier basis measurement of the input is at least as precise and uses a simpler circuit.
  For denoising, we insert a block encoded shrinkage operator between the transform and its inverse. Postselection on the shift register implements the cycle spinning average exactly as a linear combination of unitaries. Weights shared within each level give a translation equivariant filter with zero phase. Local weights also preserve translation equivariance when indexed by the nondecimated translate. The circuit provides access to individual decimated branches and combines them coherently. We illustrate the method with James Stein shrinkage, local empirical Wiener filtering, and a scaling analysis of turbulent wind velocity. Gate simulations verify the construction, and we report state preparation, weight estimation, and output costs separately.

articles.title_original: Virasoro Symmetry in Neural Network Field Theories
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2512.24420v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We construct the Virasoro algebra from a neural free-field architecture. A logarithmic momentum law and a smooth spectral window give the weight-one current kernel, whose radial-ordering discontinuity fixes the oscillator pairing. The limiting neural current correlations agree with the Fock vacuum correlations. Their Sugawara stress tensor gives the Virasoro algebra with central charge one, and charged vertex insertions identify its highest-weight sectors. Bounds on regulator and feature errors control finite-mode approximations to this representation. At finite width, an explicit adjoint-compatible projection defines an auxiliary Fock readout when its Hermitian mixed block is positive. Cauchy features extend the construction to fermionic and supersymmetric sectors, including a Clifford zero mode in the Ramond representation, while first-order stress tensors give fermionic and bosonic ghost systems. Shared reflected features impose scalar boundary conditions in every realization and yield conformal and superconformal gluing in the limiting fields. Numerical comparisons support the current pairing and field correlations; their detailed analysis is collected in the appendices.

articles.title_original: Learning Multinomial Logits in $O(n \log n)$ time
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2601.04423v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A Multinomial Logit (MNL) model is composed of a finite universe of items $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$, each assigned a positive weight. A query specifies an admissible subset---called a slate---and the model chooses one item from that slate with probability proportional to its weight. This query model is also known as the Plackett--Luce model or conditional sampling oracle in the literature. Although MNLs have been studied extensively, a basic computational question remains open: given query access to slates, how efficiently can we learn weights so that, for every slate, the induced choice distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the ground truth? This question is central to MNL learning and has direct implications for modern recommender system interfaces. We provide both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms for this task. Our first adaptive algorithm makes $O(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ queries and learns every choice distribution in total variation distance $\varepsilon$. We also provide a second adaptive algorithm that with $O(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ queries provides a stronger guarantee: each choice distribution is approximated to a multiplicative $1\pm\varepsilon$ error (except for subsets of mass smaller than $\varepsilon$). We complement these algorithms with lower bounds of $\Omega(\frac{n\log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ for total variation distance and $\Omega(\frac{n \log n}{\varepsilon^3})$ for the multiplicative error guarantee, showing the optimality of our adaptive algorithms. Our non-adaptive algorithm makes $O\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\varepsilon^{3}}\log n \log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)$ queries to obtain guarantees under the multiplicative error notion. We complement this result with an $\Omega(\frac{n^2 \log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ lower bound for any non-adaptive algorithm, showing that our algorithm is almost tight in $n$ (within a $\log n$ factor).

articles.title_original: SpikingGamma: Temporally Precise Online SNN Training Through Smoothed Temporal Delays
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.01978v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neuromorphic hardware implementations of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, low-latency AI through sparse, event-driven computation. Yet, training SNNs under fine temporal discretization remains challenging, hindering low-latency responsiveness and the mapping of software-trained SNNs to efficient hardware. In current approaches, spiking neurons are modeled as self-recurrent units, embedded into recurrent networks to maintain state over time, and trained with BPTT or RTRL variants based on surrogate gradients. These methods scale poorly with temporal resolution, while online approximations exhibit instability for long sequences and tend to fail at capturing temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we develop SpikingGamma, an SNN architecture in which neurons maintain a compact bank of smoothed-delay states and communicate through sigma-delta spike-coding. We show that in feedforward networks, SpikingGamma supports direct online error backpropagation through the continuous reconstruction signal, avoiding surrogate gradients through the spike discontinuity. This enables stable learning of temporal patterns with minimal spiking and scales feedforward SNNs to complex tasks and benchmarks with competitive accuracy, all while remaining robust to the temporal resolution of the model. Our approach offers both an alternative to recurrent SNNs trained with surrogate gradients, and a novel route for mapping SNNs to neuromorphic hardware.

articles.title_original: Anytime-Valid Conformal Risk Control
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.04364v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Prediction sets provide a means of quantifying the uncertainty in predictive tasks. Using held out calibration data, conformal prediction and risk control can produce prediction sets that exhibit statistically valid error control in a computationally efficient manner. However, in the standard formulations, the error is only controlled on average over many possible calibration datasets of fixed size. In this paper, we extend the control to remain valid with high probability over a cumulatively growing calibration dataset at any time point. We derive such guarantees using quantile-based arguments and illustrate the applicability of the proposed framework to settings involving distribution shift. We further show that our guarantees are asymptotically tight, in the sense that the risks converge to the target level from below, and that the rate of our correction cannot be improved. Finally, we demonstrate the practical performance of our methods through both simulations and real-world numerical examples.

articles.title_original: Wedge Sampling: Efficient Tensor Completion with Nearly-Linear Sample Complexity
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.05869v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce wedge sampling, a non-adaptive sampling scheme for recovering an order-$k$ low-rank tensor of side length $n$ from structured observations of its entries. The scheme samples pairs of entries in the same column of a tensor unfolding, forming length-two paths (wedges) in the associated bipartite sampling graph. The products of the paired entries supply the row correlations needed for spectral initialization in regimes where uniform sampling yields too few wedges. For fixed rank, incoherence, tensor order, and condition number, wedge sampling enables polynomial-time recovery with nearly linear sample complexity in $n$. The spectral initializer can be combined with existing refinement procedures using only an additional $\tilde O(n)$ uniformly sampled entries. Spectral refinement achieves weak recovery to any fixed relative Frobenius error. For symmetric third-order tensors with incoherent canonical polyadic factors, gradient descent achieves exact recovery in the noiseless setting, with error decreasing geometrically. The improvement over the $\tilde O(n^{k/2})$ sample complexity typical of efficient methods under uniform entry sampling shows how the conjectured computational barrier depends on the observation model. A key ingredient for the gradient descent analysis is a concentration bound for sparse random tensors in an incoherent spectral norm. We also give error bounds for both procedures under additive Gaussian noise and explicit signal-to-noise conditions. Beyond tensor completion, the same sampling scheme improves the sample complexity of one-sided matrix completion, where the goal is to recover the left singular subspace of a matrix with many more columns than rows.

articles.title_original: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.10510v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $\Theta((\varepsilon \beta)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $\beta$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.

articles.agent: アルゴリズム担当エージェント
articles.title_original: SimVLA: Attributing Gains in VLA Models Through Controlled Ablation
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2602.18224v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often bundle architectural changes with different pretraining data, backbone scales, and optimization recipes, obscuring what actually drives progress. We introduce SimVLA, a deliberately minimal VLA, a standard vision-language backbone with a lightweight continuous-action head, as a controlled testbed for this attribution problem; our contribution is methodological and empirical (a controlled attribution study and a minimal-baseline calibration), not a new technique. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, WidowX, and Google Robot, one-knob-at-a-time ablations show that training dynamics are the largest measured driver, producing performance swings of $\Delta$$\approx$54--94\%, while task configuration and architecture have smaller effects under matched settings. Despite using a small backbone and no additional large-scale robot-data VLA pretraining before benchmark-specific training, SimVLA reaches 98.6\% average success on LIBERO, remains competitive across the other benchmarks, and transfers to held-out real-robot scenes. These results suggest that simple, carefully controlled VLA baselines remain underexplored and provide a calibration point for future architectural claims within the VLM-encoder plus lightweight-head family. Website: https://frontierrobo.github.io/SimVLA

articles.title_original: Convergence Rate of a Functional Learning Method for Conditional Stochastic Optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.13048v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We consider a stochastic optimization problem involving two random variables: a context variable $X$ and a dependent variable $Y$. The objective is to minimize the expected value of a nonlinear loss functional applied to the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y,\beta) \mid X]$, where $f$ is a nonlinear function and $\beta$ represents the decision variables. We focus on the practically important setting in which direct sampling from the conditional distribution of $Y \mid X$ is infeasible, and only a stream of i.i.d. observation pairs $\{(X^k, Y^k)\}_{k=0,1,2,\ldots}$ is available. In our approach, the conditional expectation is approximated within a prespecified parametric function class. We analyze a simultaneous learning-and-optimization algorithm that jointly estimates the conditional expectation and optimizes the outer objective. Using a specially designed measure of non-optimality, combining the squared norm of the objective function's gradient and the mean square error of the auxiliary parametric model, we establish that the method achieves a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\big(1/\sqrt{N}\big)$, where $N$ denotes the number of observed pairs. The rate holds in expectation when the auxiliary model is linear in its parameters, which includes linear architectures with bounded features, and in probability for general smooth models.

articles.title_original: {\lambda}Split: Self-Supervised Content-Aware Spectral Unmixing for Fluorescence Microscopy
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.23647v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In fluorescence microscopy, spectral unmixing aims to recover individual fluorophore concentrations from spectral images that capture mixed fluorophore emissions. Since classical methods operate pixel-wise and rely on least-squares fitting, their performance degrades with increasingly overlapping emission spectra and higher levels of noise, suggesting that a data-driven approach that can learn and utilize a structural prior might lead to improved results. Learning-based approaches for spectral imaging do exist, but they are either not optimized for microscopy data or are developed for very specific cases that are not applicable to fluorescence microscopy settings. To address this, we propose {\lambda}Split, a physics-informed deep generative model that learns a conditional distribution over concentration maps using a hierarchical Variational Autoencoder. A fully differentiable Spectral Mixer enforces consistency with the image formation process, while the learned structural priors enable state-of-the-art unmixing and implicit noise removal. We demonstrate {\lambda}Split on 3 real-world datasets that we synthetically cast into a total of 66 challenging spectral unmixing benchmarks. We compare our results against a total of 10 baseline methods, including classical methods and a range of learning-based methods. Our results consistently show competitive performance and improved robustness in high noise regimes, when spectra overlap considerably, or when the spectral dimensionality is lowered, making {\lambda}Split a new state-of-the-art for spectral unmixing of fluorescent microscopy data. Importantly, {\lambda}Split is compatible with spectral data produced by standard confocal microscopes, enabling immediate adoption without specialized hardware modifications.

articles.title_original: Continuous-time learning of probability distributions: a case study in a digital trial of young children with type 1 diabetes
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.24427v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Understanding how biomarker distributions evolve over time is a central challenge in digital health and chronic disease monitoring. For example, in diabetes, changes in the distribution of glucose measurements can reveal patterns of disease progression and treatment response that conventional summary measures miss. Motivated by a 13-week clinical trial comparing the closed-loop insulin delivery system t:slim X2 with standard therapy in children with type 1 diabetes, we propose a probabilistic framework to model the continuous-time evolution of time-indexed distributions using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data collected every five minutes. We represent the glucose distribution as a Gaussian mixture, with time-varying mixture weights governed by a neural ODE. We estimate the model parameters using a distribution-matching criterion based on the maximum mean discrepancy. The resulting framework is interpretable, computationally efficient, and sensitive to subtle temporal distributional changes. In the CGM trial data analyzed here, the method detects treatment-related improvements in glucose dynamics that are difficult to capture with traditional analytical approaches.

articles.title_original: The Value of Information in Resource-Constrained Pricing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2603.24974v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Dynamic pricing with resource constraints requires balancing exploration of unknown demand patterns against exploitation of known information to maximize revenue. We develop algorithms for this problem across different information regimes. Products share perishable resources, and the firm posts prices and observes the realized requests, which may exceed the remaining capacity. In the full-information setting, a residual-correction policy that solves the fluid problem once attains $O(\log T)$ regret with bounded prices and arbitrary-rank resource matrices. In the no-information setting, deterministic exploration followed by a certainty-equivalent policy attains $O(\sqrt T)$ regret when the limiting fluid solution is nondegenerate. In the informed-price setting, given an initial price-demand estimate, a feedback controller learns the implementing prices without estimating the slope matrix if the slope matrix is symmetric, a set containing it is known in advance, the informed price is aligned with the resource constraints, and an inverse-image condition holds. A selector chooses between the informed-price algorithm and the no-information algorithm from historical data. Its regret bound includes observation error, misalignment, inventory exits, and periods on the fixed price. We further show how offline surrogate models reduce the regret of the learning policy through variance reduction, even when misspecified. The bound includes calibration and screen failures, and the regret is reduced for all sufficiently large horizons. We finally demonstrate the empirical performances of our policies through complete numerical experiments.

articles.title_original: Component-Adaptive and Lesion-Level Supervision for Improved Small Structure Segmentation in Brain MRI
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.08015v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Small lesions in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are easily missed: a segmentation model can reach a high Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) while leaving many of them undetected. We ask whether this omission comes from the network or from the training objective. In multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation, nnU-Net trained with its default Dice and cross-entropy loss produces almost no response to most of the small lesions it misses, so no decision threshold recovers them, and four other architectures trained with the same loss detect no more of them. We therefore change only the objective. CATMIL adds two lesion-level terms to the nnU-Net loss: a Component-Adaptive Tversky (CAT) term, which gives each lesion a weight nearly independent of its size, and a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) term, which treats each lesion as a bag of voxels and penalizes any lesion in which no voxel is detected. On MSLesSeg, CATMIL raises small-lesion recall from 0.796 to 0.873 (difference 95\% CI +0.030 to +0.157) and misses 48\% fewer lesions, at comparable DSC. The gain holds on the cross-validation predictions of 47 further patients, for lesions of at least 3~mm, and on a second dataset trained with the same loss weights. CATMIL also detects more small lesions than CC-DiceCE, an instance-level loss that balances lesions within an overlap term (0.873 vs.\ 0.831), indicating that lesions must be supervised not only in proportion but also for their detection. The cost is additional small false-positive components; a component-size filter removes most of them, and at the lesion-wise precision of the default loss CATMIL still detects more small lesions. Code: https://github.com/luumsk/SmallLesionMRI.

articles.title_original: OpenTME: An Open Dataset of AI-powered H&E Tumor Microenvironment Profiles from TCGA
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.12075v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a central role in cancer progression, treatment response, and patient outcomes, yet large-scale, consistent, and quantitative TME characterization from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histopathology remains scarce. We introduce OpenTME, an open-access dataset of pre-computed TME profiles derived from 5,268 H&E-stained whole-slide images across ten cancer types (bladder, breast, colorectal, head and neck, liver, lung, ovarian, pancreatic, prostate, and stomach cancer) from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). All outputs were generated using HETA (H&E Tissue Analysis), an AI-powered application built on the Atlas family of pathology foundation models, which performs tissue quality control, tissue segmentation, cell detection and classification, tumor zone and tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) detection, and spatial neighborhood analysis, yielding over 20,000 quantitative readouts per slide at cell-level resolution, including curated features such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, tumor mitotic index, or mature TLS counts. OpenTME is available for non-commercial academic research on Hugging Face. We will continue to expand OpenTME over time and anticipate it will serve as a resource for biomarker discovery, spatial biology research, and the development of computational methods for TME analysis.

articles.title_original: Optimal algorithmic complexity of inference in quantum kernel methods
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.15214v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Quantum kernel methods are among the leading candidates for achieving quantum advantage in supervised learning. A key bottleneck is the cost of inference: evaluating a trained model on new data requires estimating a weighted sum $\sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i k(x,x_i)$ of $N$ kernel values to additive precision $\varepsilon$, where $\alpha$ is the vector of trained coefficients. The standard approach estimates each term independently via sampling, yielding a query complexity of $O(N\lVert\alpha\rVert_2^2/\varepsilon^2)$. In this work, we identify two independent axes for improvement: (1) How individual kernel values are estimated (sampling versus quantum amplitude estimation), and (2) how the sum is approximated (term-by-term versus via a single observable), and systematically analyze all combinations thereof. The query-optimal combination, encoding the full inference sum as the expectation value of a single observable and applying quantum amplitude estimation, achieves a query complexity of $O(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1/\varepsilon)$, removing the dependence on $N$ from the query count and yielding a quadratic improvement in both $\lVert\alpha\rVert_1$ and $\varepsilon$. We prove a matching lower bound of $\Omega(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1/\varepsilon)$, establishing query-optimality of our approach up to logarithmic factors. Beyond query complexity, we also analyze how these improvements translate into gate costs and show that the query-optimal strategy is not always optimal in practice from the perspective of gate complexity. Our results provide both a query-optimal algorithm and a practically optimal choice of strategy depending on hardware capabilities, along with a complete landscape of intermediate methods to guide practitioners. All algorithms require only amplitude estimation as a subroutine and are thus natural candidates for early-fault-tolerant implementations.

articles.title_original: Learning Curves and Prediction Persistence to Under-Regularization of Spectral Algorithms in Large Dimensions
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2604.23212v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study how prediction risk changes as regularization is reduced for spectral algorithms when the sample size $n$ and dimension $d$ satisfy $n\asymp d^\gamma$ for fixed $\gamma>0$. For inner-product kernels on the sphere, under a source condition with smoothness $s\geq0$ and a signal nondegeneracy condition, we characterize the conditional excess risk up to constant factors at each fixed admissible scale $\lambda\asymp d^{-u}$, $u>0$, and at interpolation. The resulting risk orders describe the effects of source smoothness, filter qualification, and transitions between spectral blocks. They identify when the conditional excess risk retains the minimax risk order as regularization is weakened from an optimal scale to interpolation, and when an interval before interpolation exhibits a polynomially larger risk. We also compare the kernel risk with a population sequence risk for the same spectral filter, using a deterministic regularization scale bounded below by order $n^{-1}$. Finally, for noninteger $\gamma$, we extend the risk characterization for kernel ridge regression to kernels on general domains under spectral scaling, hyper-contractivity, and tail diagonal concentration conditions, together with the source and signal conditions.

articles.title_original: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Benchmarking Super-Resolution Models for Large-Scale Remote Sensing Imagery via Downstream Task Integration
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.00310v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Super-resolution (SR) techniques have made major advances in reconstructing high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs. The increased resolution provides visual enhancement and utility for monitoring tasks. In particular, SR has been increasingly developed for satellite-based Earth observation, with applications in urban planning, agriculture, ecology, and disaster response. However, existing SR studies and benchmarks typically use fidelity metrics such as PSNR or SSIM, whereas the true utility of super-resolved images lies in supporting downstream tasks such as land cover classification, biomass estimation, and change detection. To bridge this gap, we introduce GeoSR-Bench, a downstream task-integrated SR benchmark dataset to evaluate SR models beyond fidelity metrics. GeoSR-Bench comprises spatially co-located, temporally aligned, and quality-controlled image pairs from about 36,000 locations across diverse land covers, spanning resolutions from 500m to 0.6m. To the best of our knowledge, GeoSR-Bench is the first SR benchmark that directly connects improved image resolution from SR models with downstream Earth monitoring tasks, including land cover segmentation, infrastructure mapping, and biophysical variable estimation. Using GeoSR-Bench, we benchmark GAN, transformer, neural operator, and diffusion-based SR models on perceptual quality and downstream task performance. We conduct experiments with 270 settings, covering 2 cross-platform SR tasks, 9 SR models, 3 downstream task models, and 5 downstream tasks for each SR task. The results show that improvements in traditional SR metrics often do not correlate with gains in task performance, and the correlations can be negative, indicating that these metrics provide limited guidance for selecting superior models for downstream tasks. This reveals the need to integrate downstream tasks into SR model development and evaluation.

articles.title_original: Gradient Regularized Newton Boosting Trees with Global Convergence
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.00581v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) dominate tabular machine learning, with modern implementations like XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost being based on Newton boosting: a second-order descent step in the space of decision trees. Despite its empirical success, the global convergence of Newton boosting is poorly understood compared to first-order boosting. In this paper, we introduce Restricted Newton Descent, a framework for convex optimization with Newton's method on Hilbert spaces with inexact iterates, based on the concepts of cosine angle and weak gradient edge. Within this framework, we recover Newton boosting with GBDTs and classical finite-dimensional theory as special cases. We first prove that vanilla Newton boosting achieves a linear rate of convergence for smooth, strongly convex losses that satisfy a Hessian-dominance condition. To handle general convex losses with Lipschitz Hessians, we extend a recent gradient regularized Newton scheme to the restricted weak learner setting, establishing the first global $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k^2})$ convergence rate for second-order GBDTs. This scheme minimally modifies the classical algorithm by introducing an adaptive $\ell_2$-regularization term proportional to the square root of the gradient norm at each iteration. In numerical experiments, we show that this scheme converges while vanilla Newton boosting may diverge.

articles.title_original: Structured Role-Aware Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.07274v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), especially with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has shown strong potential for improving the reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs). However, in multimodal reasoning, final-answer rewards are typically assigned at the sequence level and do not distinguish the functional roles of different tokens, making it difficult to determine whether a correct answer is supported by task-relevant visual evidence. In this paper, we revisit multimodal RLVR from the perspective of role-aware token-level credit assignment, where structured responses are decomposed into perception tokens for extracting visual evidence and reasoning tokens for deriving answers from that evidence. Based on this perspective, we propose Structured Role-aware Policy Optimization (SRPO), which refines the sequence-level GRPO advantage into role-aware token-level advantages without changing the reward function. Specifically, SRPO assigns role-specific credit by using self-distilled on-policy contrasts: perception tokens are emphasized according to their visual dependency under original versus corrupted visual inputs, while reasoning tokens are emphasized according to their consistency with the generated perception. These role-specific signals are further unified through a shared trajectory-level baseline, yielding positive token weights that adjust relative update magnitudes while preserving the original GRPO reward and advantage signs, without requiring external reward models or separate teachers. Experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that SRPO improves evidence-grounded reasoning, highlighting the importance of moving beyond uniform sequence-level credit toward role-aware optimization for reliable multimodal reasoning.

articles.title_original: Survey-aware Machine Learning: A Guideline for Valid Population Health Inference based on Scoping Review
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.08963v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models trained on complex health surveys such as the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) often ignore primary sampling units, stratification variables, and sampling weights. This practice violates the independence assumptions of standard evaluation methods. As a result, estimates become biased, uncertainty is underestimated, and fairness assessments fail to reflect population-level disparities. We propose Survey-aware Machine Learning (SaML), a nine-step guideline that incorporates survey design metadata across the ML lifecycle. Through a scoping review of 16 methodological papers, we summarize existing work on weighted model training, design-based cross-validation, and survey-adjusted performance evaluation. We also identify gaps in hyperparameter tuning and deployment. We provide task-specific guidance that clarifies which steps are required for different analytical objectives. SaML provides a checklist for valid population inference from survey data.

articles.title_original: Insights Generator: Systematic Corpus-Level Trace Diagnostics for LLM Agents
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.21347v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Diagnosing failures in LLM agents remains largely manual. Practitioners inspect a small subset of execution traces, form ad-hoc hypotheses, and iterate. This process misses patterns that only emerge across trace populations and does not scale to production corpora where individual traces span tens of thousands of tokens. We formalize the problem of corpus-level trace diagnostics. Given a corpus of execution traces, the goal is to produce grounded natural-language insights that characterize systematic behavioral patterns across trace groups, each linked to supporting evidence. We present the Insights Generator (IG), a multi-agent system that answers diagnostic questions by proposing and testing hypotheses across the trace corpus to produce an evidence-backed insights report. We evaluate IG across qualitative and objective dimensions, spanning rubric-based report assessment and downstream performance improvements achieved by implementing IG insights. Human experts using IG reports improve scaffold performance by 30.4 pp over the unmodified baseline scaffold, and coding agents leveraging IG-derived insights show consistent and stable gains. Across benchmarks, IG's scout-investigator architecture produces findings comparable in detection coverage to competing approaches, while domain experts rated IG reports as leading depth and evidence quality.

articles.title_original: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.29486v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Real applications provide the training setting closest to phone-agent deployment, but are difficult to reset, scale safely, and verify programmatically. Static screenshots and interaction trajectories preserve realistic evidence but cannot generate new experience. We introduce PhoneWorld, a trace-grounded framework that converts such evidence into runnable, resettable, and verifiable Android environments. PhoneWorld induces a usage-weighted interaction skeleton from observed pages, transitions, and state-changing operations; translates it into a behavior-grounded app specification; realizes the specification through an autonomous build--inspect--repair loop; and synthesizes executable tasks with programmatic verifiers. The resulting suite spans 34 consumer-facing apps across 16 domains and supports an audited online benchmark, verified trajectory generation, and online RL through common reset and verification interfaces. Evaluations with diverse general and open-source GUI agents show that PhoneWorld supports reliable end-to-end online interaction and exposes capabilities complementary to AndroidWorld. Controlled SFT experiments further show that PhoneWorld trajectories complement AndroidWorld supervision, transfer across online and offline benchmarks, and become more effective as data volume and app coverage increase. Under a matched RL budget, combining PhoneWorld mock-app rollouts with real-app rollouts improves performance over real-app RL alone on both real-phone tasks and AndroidWorld. Together, these results demonstrate that trace-grounded executable abstraction can bridge realistic mobile behavior and scalable agent learning, turning limited real-app evidence into a growing supply of controllable and verifiable environments for training and evaluation.

articles.title_original: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.00384v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Fitting quantitative models to data is a central step in scientific workflows, yet it remains one of the least automated. Recent agent-based systems leverage language and vision-language models (VLMs) to propose statistical models, but these systems struggle on challenging modeling tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce VESTA (Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents), a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing toolkit to guide model refinement through data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, and statistical tests. Unlike prior systems that rely on iterative critique alone, VESTA explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating reusable diagnostic tools. We evaluate VESTA using three toolkit configurations: no tools, static expert-written tools, and dynamic model-written tools. To support this evaluation, we introduce DAWN (Dataset for Automated Workflows and Numerical Modeling), a benchmark targeting distribution fitting and time series modeling with varying difficulty tiers that culminates in real-world astronomy tasks including modeling initial mass functions and gravitational-wave chirp signals. VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines for statistical analysis and visual tool creation, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks. Against strong agentic coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode), VESTA is better on all time series tasks and on complex distribution fitting tasks, though the harnesses achieve better fits on simpler distributions. Further, dynamically generated tools are substantially more sophisticated than those produced by existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and strongly preferring visual outputs that the VESTA VLM critic can reason over directly.

articles.title_original: Adaptive Inference for Resource-Constrained Dynamic Pricing
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.03736v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study dynamic pricing over a finite selling horizon when limited resource capacity determines revenue and the observations available for inference at a prespecified price. Resource depletion can remove the target neighborhood from the feasible price set, changing the experiment generated by the pricing policy. We develop inference-aware re-solving controllers that check target-band feasibility before current covariates arrive and log the pricing mixture. Target-reserved and smooth controllers take population mean-pair geometry as a predeployment input; learned barycentric re-solving instead estimates stationary mean-consumption vectors of predeclared component kernels. On an affine binding-capacity family, an exact-input target-reserved controller assigning mass $t^{-\gamma}$ obtains an information clock of order $T^{1-\gamma}$ in probability, radius $O_p\{T^{-(1-\gamma)/2}\}$, and, under an exposed-face reward identity, a signed fluid-benchmark gap bounded above by $O(\log T+T^{1-\gamma})$. Under the exogenous affine-face condition, predeclared target support, and polynomial error spending with exponent greater than one, learned barycentric re-solving has a linear information clock in probability and an $O(\log T)$ signed-gap upper bound; centered local pricing has the same orders under slack capacity and global target optimality. An exact-input, target-compatible smooth alternative without reservation gives a linear clock in probability, an $O_p(T^{-1/2})$ deterministic-envelope radius with unconditional coverage and reporting probability tending to one, and an $O(\log^2 T)$ signed-gap upper bound. Boundary results show when physical support is lost and why a $1/t$ target branch yields only $O_p(1)$ information if it is the sole target-local source. The policy reports an interval when its prespecified support and information conditions hold and otherwise abstains.
